text:
$NVDA $TSM TSMC AND NVIDIA: THE DIVISION OF LABOR AFTER THE JENSEN TRANSITION

The most critical operational learning from NVIDIA's Q3 FY27 earnings call on 11/17/26 was not a number. It was a name: TSMC.

THE TELL FROM THE CALL

Answering Vivek Arya's question on what stays durable through the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress said: "I see right now the leadership, even from TSMC, that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us. We secured memory. We secured advanced packaging."

The sentence was not in prepared remarks. It was offered, in a governance answer, as evidence that the company's moat survives the founder's exit. Of every institution Kress could have named, she named the foundry, and she named it at the level of "leadership in our offices this week," meaning the engagement is executive to executive during the transition week itself, not a standing purchase order.

The same day, NVIDIA published its supply-chain release, "NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout." In it, TSMC SVP and deputy co-COO Dr. Kevin Zhang is quoted: "TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation. This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market." The release states that Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 leveraging TSMC's 5nm, 3nm, and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Zhang is the right name to notice: he is TSMC's senior executive for the technology and packaging side of the customer relationship, and his April 2026 public remarks confirmed TSMC will build advanced packaging capacity (CoWoS and 3D-IC) in Arizona before 2029, moving TSMC from pure wafer foundry toward localized one-stop service for NVIDIA and Apple.

HOW A FOUNDRY CARRIES A FABLESS ROADMAP

TSMC's support for NVIDIA's roadmap is not generic capacity. It operates through five concrete mechanisms.

First, custom process variants built for NVIDIA alone. NVIDIA's own architecture pages state that Blackwell GPUs are "manufactured using a custom-built TSMC 4NP process," and NVIDIA's Hopper technical blog states the GH100 was "fabricated using the TSMC 4N process customized for NVIDIA." 4N was a variant of TSMC's N4 tuned for NVIDIA; 4NP refined it. A foundry does not build a named, customer-specific process flavor for a customer it treats as interchangeable. This is design-technology co-optimization in its most literal form: the process design kit, transistor tuning, and yield learning are accumulated against NVIDIA's reticle-limit dies (Blackwell is two dies, 208 billion transistors), and that accumulated learning is not transferable to another vendor on any useful timeline.

Second, node sequencing locked years ahead. Vera Rubin ships on TSMC 3nm-class process (reported as N3P, a refined 3nm variant, paired with CoWoS-L packaging), with networking and other platform silicon on 5nm. Rubin Ultra follows in 2027. For Feynman (2028), multiple supply-chain reports say NVIDIA will be the first, and reportedly the only, customer for TSMC's A16 node, whose defining feature is Super Power Rail backside power delivery, worth a claimed 8 to 10% speed gain at the same voltage or 15 to 20% power reduction at the same speed against N2P per TSMC's own symposium figures. Apple is reported to skip A16 entirely and go from N2 to A14. The significance for the transition question: the Feynman decision, if the reports are right, was made inside the Huang era and binds NVIDIA to TSMC's most experimental node for 2028. Whoever the permanent CEO is, the silicon roadmap through 2028 is already a TSMC joint program. One counterweight: DigiTimes has reported NVIDIA exploring Intel EMIB packaging for a minority share (reported around 25%) of Feynman packaging, with the balance at TSMC. That reporting is single-source and unconfirmed. Even if true, it diversifies a packaging step, not the wafer or the roadmap relationship.

The CPU leg of the roadmap runs through the same channel. The 11/17/26 release states that Vera CPUs, not only Rubin GPUs, began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 on TSMC process and CoWoS technologies. Management expects standalone CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028 as Vera moves from the Grace pattern (a CPU paired inside a Grace Blackwell or Vera Rubin system) toward a merchant CPU sold across cloud operators and AI customers for agent execution and orchestration workloads. That expansion is entirely fabless: every incremental Vera CPU is a TSMC wafer and, in its packaged form, CoWoS capacity. TSMC's side has publicly leaned into the same theme, with Wei's Q2 2026 call remarks on agentic CPU demand. For the transition question this matters because the CPU is the newest and least Huang-dependent leg of the roadmap: its ramp is a manufacturing and packaging execution problem of exactly the kind TSMC underwrites, rather than a founder-vision problem.

Third, CoWoS allocation as the shipment governor. Advanced packaging, not wafer starts, is the binding constraint on AI accelerator shipments. TSMC's CoWoS capacity ran about 13,000 to 16,000 wafers per month in 2023, about 70,000 by end of 2025, is expected to exceed 130,000 per month by end of 2026, and to reach roughly 170,000 to 200,000 per month in 2027 depending on the estimating house (KGI at 170k, UBS at about 180k for TSMC within a 270k industry total, other supply chain estimates above 200k). Morgan Stanley's supply chain survey puts NVIDIA's share of global CoWoS demand at about 60% in 2026, easing to about 45% in 2027 as hyperscaler ASICs grow; UBS puts NVIDIA's share of CoWoS wafer demand at 65% in 2025 falling to 49% in 2027. NVIDIA is reported to have booked about 595,000 CoWoS wafers for 2026, roughly 515,000 of them from TSMC, the bulk CoWoS-L for Rubin, Vera CPUs, and GB-series parts. One arithmetic tension in the source set: 515,000 wafers against the capacity path above implies roughly 40 to 45% of TSMC's 2026 CoWoS output, below the roughly 60% demand-share survey figure. The two series most likely measure different things (surveyed demand versus booked or allocated wafers), so they should not be combined arithmetically; either way, NVIDIA is the pool's largest single claimant by a wide margin. C.C. Wei has said on an investor call that packaging capacity was "so tight that it limited customer growth." When Kress says "we secured advanced packaging," this is the asset she means: allocation inside a capacity pool that will not clear demand until 2027 at the earliest, allocated by TSMC, to the customer TSMC chooses to prioritize.

Fourth, yield and ramp co-management. Vera Rubin generated nearly $20 billion of revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, the fastest ramp in NVIDIA's history. A ramp of that slope on a new platform, a new memory generation (HBM4), and CoWoS-L packaging is a joint NVIDIA-TSMC engineering exercise: defect density learning on reticle-scale dies, interposer supply (including the GlobalFoundries silicon interposer agreement inside the CoWoS ecosystem), and substrate capacity, which is why the 11/17/26 release also carries Kinsus expanding NVIDIA-dedicated substrate capacity by more than 3.5x and SPIL expanding advanced packaging under multiyear agreement with multibillion-dollar NVIDIA funding. TSMC's role in a ramp is the unglamorous one that decides whether a launch quarter is a beat or a miss: it owns the yield curve.

Fifth, capacity underwriting through prepayment and commitment structures on both sides. NVIDIA's supply commitments rose from $279 billion to $390 billion in one quarter, primarily multi-year memory procurement, inside $518 billion of all-in commitments. On the capital-allocation question, Kress ranked supplier prepaids as the top operating use of capital after buybacks. TSMC's side of the same structure is its capex: the 2026 budget stands at $60 to $64 billion, with Deutsche Bank's October 2026 forecasts putting 2027 capex at $84 billion and 2028 at $100 billion (single-source analyst estimates). Wei's stated discipline is that he verifies demand personally before spending: "I want to make sure that my customers' demand are real. So I talked to those cloud service providers, all of them... they show me the evidence that the AI really helps their business." The mechanism, in one sentence: NVIDIA prepays and commits, TSMC builds and allocates, and each side's balance sheet now carries the other's forecast.

WHAT TSMC HAS AT STAKE

NVIDIA is now TSMC's largest customer. Analyst estimates carried by CNBC in January 2026 put NVIDIA at roughly $33 billion of TSMC revenue in 2026, about 22% of the total, against Apple's roughly $27 billion and 18%, and Huang himself confirmed the ranking on a podcast ("Morris will be happy to know NVIDIA is TSMC's largest customer now"). TSMC does not publish customer-level revenue, so the percentages are estimates, while the ranking is confirmed by Huang's own statement. One vintage warning on those figures: the January 2026 estimates imply a TSMC 2026 revenue total near $150 billion, but TSMC has since blown past that path, with Q3 2026 revenue of about $46.7 billion, Q4 guided to $52.3 to $54.3 billion, and full-year growth guidance raised to around 44%. On the current run rate, $33 billion would be a materially smaller share than 22%, so either the dollar figure is now stale and too low if the share held, or the share has eased as the rest of the HPC complex grew. The ranking is confirmed; the exact 2026 share is not. TSMC's disclosed platform mix shows the concentration underneath: HPC was 68% of revenue in Q3 2026, and NVIDIA is the largest single contributor to that platform.

The Arizona program prices the stake. TSMC's US commitment stood at $165 billion (six fabs, two advanced packaging facilities, an R&D center) after the March 2025 addition of $100 billion. At the Q2 2026 earnings call, Wei announced a further $100 billion US investment, taking the Arizona total to $265 billion across 12 facilities, with dedicated CoWoS packaging capacity in Arizona aimed at the AI packaging bottleneck. Arizona's anchor demand is US AI and HPC customers; the campus exists because NVIDIA-class demand made US leading-edge capacity financeable, and its economics depend on that demand persisting at high utilization for decades. Advanced packaging is becoming a P&L line in its own right: UBS expects advanced packaging and testing to reach about 12% of TSMC's sales in 2026 and 16% in 2027.

The exposure is symmetric and already visible in the tape. On 11/16/26, before NVIDIA had reported anything, Asia sold the supply chain on the NVIDIA CEO story: the Taiex fell 6.03%, its second-largest point drop on record, and TSMC fell 5.74% (exchange figures relayed across multiple accounts; treat as color, consistent across sources). TSMC's equity is, in part, a derivative of NVIDIA's stability. If NVIDIA stumbles, TSMC does not merely lose orders: it holds CoWoS capacity built for one customer's package architecture, N3 and A16 capacity sequenced around one customer's roadmap, and an Arizona gigafab cluster whose utilization case is AI demand concentrated in a handful of US customers, NVIDIA first among them. Wei's own hedge is the rest of the HPC complex (AMD, Broadcom, the hyperscaler ASIC programs all ride the same CoWoS pool, which is why NVIDIA's share falls toward 45 to 49% by 2027 even as its absolute wafers grow), plus Apple on the consumer side. But there is no second NVIDIA: no other customer accounts for roughly 60% of global CoWoS demand in the Morgan Stanley survey or anchors a custom-node program.

This is the factual core underneath the claim that "they won't let $1tr of new fabs get mothballed." The trillion-dollar figure is best understood at industry scale rather than as a TSMC line item: announced US semiconductor investment since 2020 exceeds $828 billion across 160 projects (Semiconductor Industry Association figures), TSMC's own Arizona program is $265 billion, and TSMC's annual capex is on a path from $60 to $64 billion in 2026 toward a Deutsche Bank-estimated $100 billion by 2028. The fab complex being built on the assumption of NVIDIA-shaped demand is, in aggregate, of the order named. The incentive conclusion follows from the arithmetic, not from sentiment: TSMC's return on this buildout requires NVIDIA to keep shipping, so TSMC's rational move in a NVIDIA leadership crisis is exactly what Kress described, maximum engagement, senior people in the room, capacity and engineering support visibly committed.

TESTING THE DIVISION OF LABOR

The framing: TSMC underwrites the silicon side (process, packaging, manufacturing engineering, roadmap execution support) while NVIDIA's executive attention concentrates on land, power, and shell (neocloud financing, guarantees, prepaids, allocation by site readiness).

WHERE IT HOLDS

The call's own evidence sorts mostly along this line, with one correction. The TSMC facts Kress offered were leadership engaged and packaging secured, plus Rubin ramping at a record pace on TSMC 5nm, 3nm, and CoWoS. Memory is not a TSMC fact: TSMC does not supply HBM. NVIDIA secures HBM from its memory vendors separately (the $390 billion supply-commitment jump was primarily multi-year memory procurement), and TSMC's role is to integrate that HBM into the package through CoWoS. Conflating the two overstates TSMC's remit; the accurate claim is that TSMC underwrites the logic dies and the packaging into which separately secured memory is assembled. Every hard fact about NVIDIA's own executive work on the call was an infrastructure fact: $390 billion of supply commitments, $518 billion all-in, up to $118 billion of guarantee exposure dominated by $105 billion of SB Energy credit support, and the allocation answer, in which NVIDIA allocates its scarce output by the customer's land, power, and shell readiness and capital readiness, at uniform pricing. NVIDIA is behaving, at the top of the house, like the underwriter and allocator of an infrastructure buildout; TSMC is behaving like the guarantor of the silicon roadmap underneath it. The FY28 outlook raise to about 75% growth, delivered by an interim CEO six days into the job, is only credible if the supply side is someone else's solved problem; Kress's TSMC sentence is where she told you whose.

WHERE IT OVERSTATES

Three corrections. First, the silicon side is not outsourced in the way the framing can imply: NVIDIA still designs everything. The architectures (Rubin, Rubin Ultra, Feynman), the Vera CPU, the NVLink and networking roadmap (networking revenue above $21 billion in Q3), and the platform definitions are NVIDIA's, and TSMC has no ability to originate them. What TSMC underwrites is manufacturability and execution: that a designed part can be built, at yield, at volume, on schedule. Second, TSMC's engagement is not NVIDIA-specific charity; it is the foundry model working as designed for its largest customer, and the same CoWoS pool serves Broadcom, AMD, and the ASIC programs that compete with NVIDIA. TSMC will guarantee the ship is steady because the ship is roughly a fifth of its revenue on the January-vintage estimates, not because it has adopted NVIDIA's strategy. Third, the division is not new this week. The 4N custom process dates to Hopper (2022); what changed on 11/17/26 is that NVIDIA's interim leadership said the quiet part on an earnings call, because for the first time the question "who holds this company together operationally" was asked in public and the honest answer had a name.

WHAT TSMC CANNOT REPLACE

• CUDA and the software stack. The moat is a developer ecosystem, not a process node; TSMC has no software business.
• Systems architecture: NVL72 rack-scale design, NVLink fabric, the Spectrum and ConnectX networking line, and the CPU-GPU platform integration that makes Vera Rubin a system rather than a chip.
• Product definition and pricing: the allocation and uniform-pricing decisions Kress described are commercial acts only NVIDIA can perform.
• Customer and ecosystem capital: the guarantees, prepaids, and neocloud support structures are NVIDIA balance-sheet instruments TSMC neither offers nor could credibly replicate.
• Demand creation itself: TSMC sells capacity to whoever designs winning silicon; it cannot make the market want NVIDIA's.

If NVIDIA's design organization faltered, TSMC's capacity would migrate to AMD, Broadcom, and the hyperscaler ASICs within a few quarters, which is precisely the limit of the "taking over from the inside" thesis: TSMC can keep NVIDIA's roadmap manufacturable through a transition, and it has every incentive to, but it cannot be NVIDIA.

One further limit cuts the other way, against NVIDIA: the division of labor deepens a single-point concentration. Arizona advanced packaging arrives only before 2029 on Zhang's April 2026 remarks, so through the Rubin and Rubin Ultra ramps the CoWoS pool that governs NVIDIA's shipments remains overwhelmingly Taiwan-based. TSMC's engagement removes execution risk from the transition; it does not diversify the geography of the supply chain NVIDIA now depends on more explicitly than before.

VERDICT ON THE THREE CLAIMS

• "It looks like TSMC is taking over from the inside." Overstates if read as control, and is accurate if read as load-bearing: the operational continuity of NVIDIA currently runs through Hsinchu to a degree no other supplier relationship in the industry matches.
• "They won't let $1tr of new fabs get mothballed." Directionally right on incentives and roughly right on scale at industry level.
• "TSMC will guarantee the NVDA ship is steady and moving forward for as long as needed." The strongest of the three as stated: it is exactly what TSMC's revenue concentration, capex commitments, and Kress's account of this week's engagement describe, with one amendment. "For as long as needed" lasts only while NVIDIA keeps designing parts the market wants. The guarantee covers execution, not relevance.

THE REACTION

The TSMC line was extracted from the call within minutes and framed as a headline fact. Nicholas Mugalli (RealNickMugalli) led his call summary: "KRESS REVEALS TSMC LEADERSHIP VISITED NVIDIA'S OFFICES THIS WEEK AND IS FULLY ENGAGED IN SUPPORTING THE TRANSITION (NVDA, TSM)," bundled with "business as usual" and "suppliers and partners 100% behind the company." The Transcript (TheTranscript_) singled the same moment out as a standalone observation: Kress "casually name-dropped that the TSMC leadership was at NVIDIA's offices just this week." The read on X, in other words, matched this one: of everything said on the call, the TSMC sentence was the one the earnings-call transcription community treated as news. Broader post-earnings summaries led with the 75% FY28 raise and the $390 billion commitments rather than the TSMC angle, and the pre-print record shows the other side of the stake, the 11/16/26 Asia selloff on the CEO story. No informed channel source in this sweep contradicted the engagement account; no TSMC-side statement beyond Zhang's release quote has appeared as of this writing. The sweep covered keyword searches on the call window, not an exhaustive timeline pull.

OPEN QUESTIONS

• The exact CoWoS capacity and NVIDIA allocation figures are analyst estimates; TSMC does not disclose them. The 2027 NVIDIA share range (45 to 49%) is a two-house estimate band, not a fact.
• Whether Feynman is in fact an A16 design, and whether any Feynman packaging goes to Intel EMIB, rests on Taiwan supply-chain reporting and one DigiTimes item. NVIDIA and TSMC have not confirmed either.
• The Arizona total: $165 billion is the documented figure; the step to $265 billion rests on Q2 2026 call reporting. TSMC's own release text for the increment was not read firsthand in this research.
• NVIDIA's exact share of TSMC 2026 revenue is unresolved, for the vintage reason given above. The largest-customer ranking is confirmed; the current share is not measured by any source found.
• Whether TSMC's engagement includes any formal engineering secondment or joint task force inside NVIDIA (as distinct from executive visits and standing joint development) is not in any source found; Kress's sentence supports presence and engagement, not an organizational chart.

text:
Your Florida house spent six months without you. 🌴

Want to see what it got up to?

Every fall our phone rings with the same story. A homeowner flies back to Wellington or Royal Palm Beach and finds a surprise:
🌀 A lanai screen shredded in a summer storm
🥵 An AC that quit in August (hello, mold)
📰 A pile of flyers telling the whole street nobody was home

Here's the lesson: a seasonal home isn't at risk because it's empty. It's at risk because nobody's there to notice.

Snowbird Mode fixes that:
✅ Cameras on the driveway and front door
✅ A monitored alarm with battery and cellular backup
✅ Temperature and flood sensors that alert you before small problems get big
✅ Separate codes for the pool guy, the landscaper and the house-watcher, so you can see who came and went

Alarm or cameras? You need both. Each one covers what the other misses.

CSS Man offered to fly north with you and check on the house from the air. We went with the app instead. 🦸

text:
I don’t have the background to know how Starlink would work for air traffic controllers, so I asked Grok 

Moderately feasible as a complementary/backup system, especially for remote areas; low-to-moderate as a primary replacement for ground-based ATC in the continental U.S.
Starlink (SpaceX’s LEO constellation) offers high-speed, relatively low-latency broadband with near-global coverage. It is already being tested by the FAA and is used commercially in aviation for passenger connectivity. It is not a ready drop-in replacement for the mature ground-based systems that handle the bulk of U.S. air traffic control.
Current Real-World Status
The FAA has tested Starlink terminals at facilities including Atlantic City (lab), multiple sites in Alaska (often non-safety-critical for weather data and pilot flight services), Oklahoma, and others—reporting dozens of connections in some periods. SpaceX has provided kits at no cost for testing, working through existing contractors such as L3Harris.
The FAA has repeatedly stated that modernization requires multiple technologies (fiber, wireless, and satellite) and that Starlink is “part of the solution,” not a full replacement. No Starlink systems have been connected to the core safety-critical ATC network as primary links. Verizon holds (or held primary role in) the major FAA Enterprise Network Services (FENS) contract (~$2.4 billion, multi-year) to modernize the terrestrial backbone that supports facilities, radar data, voice, and other services. Recent developments include AT&T taking a larger role in the network overhaul.
Space-based surveillance already exists separately via Aireon (ADS-B receivers on Iridium NEXT satellites). It provides certified global coverage over oceans and remote areas where ground radar/ADS-B cannot reach, with low latency suitable for separation services. The FAA has evaluated and partnered on this data. Dedicated concepts for space-based VHF voice/data also exist in early stages.
Technical Comparison
Aspect
Starlink (LEO)
Ground-Based Systems (Radar, VHF, Fiber, ADS-B towers)
Notes
Coverage
Excellent global, including oceans, poles, remote Alaska
Strong over populated land; gaps over oceans, mountains, sparse areas
Starlink’s biggest advantage
Latency
Typically 20–50+ ms median; can spike during handoffs (~every 15 s)
Very low and stable for fiber/microwave inter-facility links; VHF voice is essentially real-time
FAA critical services (radar data, controller-pilot voice) often specify ≤50 ms. Spikes are a concern for safety-critical real-time use
Bandwidth
High (hundreds of Mbps possible)
High on modern fiber; specialized lower-bandwidth channels for legacy systems
Good for data, weather, backups
Reliability
High but commercial-grade; weather (rain fade on Ka/Ku), constellation health, potential congestion
Proven safety-of-life track record in covered areas; aging infrastructure is a known problem
Needs rigorous certification for primary ATC
Deployment
Fast, minimal ground infrastructure
Expensive and slow to build/maintain dense networks
Advantage for hard-to-reach sites
Cost
Lower CapEx for remote sites; ongoing service fees
High maintenance on legacy systems; fiber upgrades are costly but low ongoing latency
Hybrid often most economical
Integration
General IP connectivity
Specialized standards (VHF, Mode S, specific data links, automation interfaces)
Aircraft would need certified satcom equipment for air-ground primary use
Key Feasibility Factors
Strong cases for Starlink:
•Backup or primary links for remote FAA facilities (Alaska is a clear use case already being pursued).
•Redundancy against terrestrial outages (recent ground stops have highlighted vulnerability of aging networks).
•High-bandwidth data services, weather dissemination, and future aircraft datalinks in oceanic or sparse regions.
•Rapid augmentation while the multi-year FENS terrestrial upgrade proceeds.
Significant hurdles for primary use:

There’s more but there’s a limit

text:
I PUT THREE BULLETS IN MY MOM. I’VE GOT THREE MORE FOR MY STEPDAD.

That’s what a 14-year-old had already decided by the time a friend walked into her house. Her mother was on the floor in the next room.

March 19, 2024. A home camera in Rankin County, Mississippi picks up that same girl walking in from school next to her mom. An ordinary afternoon.

A few minutes later the camera catches her in the hallway, a .357 revolver tucked behind her back. Three times she pulls the trigger.

Then she grabs her mother’s phone and texts her stepdad: “Honey, when are you going to be home?”

An hour passes. He steps through the door. She’s already there, waiting behind the curtains.

The clip below is the family’s own cameras, start to finish: the walk home from school, the revolver hidden behind her, the shots, the stepdad arriving, the girl bolting out the door.

Her name is Carly Gregg. Her mother, Ashley Smylie, was 40 and taught at the very school Carly attended.

The revolver sat under the mattress, on her mom’s side of the bed. On the footage Carly leans into the kitchen first, checking her mother isn’t there, then walks back to her own bedroom, where Ashley was waiting for her.

Prosecutors say that once it was done, she video-called classmates and turned the camera on her mother’s body. Then a friend came to the house. By his account, that’s when she said it: “I put three in my mom. I’ve got three more for my stepdad.”

Heath Smylie walked in and she put a round in his shoulder. He fought the gun out of her hands. She went over the fence and ran. An officer picked her up on a road nearby. He asked if she had anything to do with the shooting. She said yes.

She was offered 40 years in a plea deal and said no, taking it to trial instead. Her lawyers argued she was hearing voices and that her new medication had tipped her over. The state built the opposite picture: a girl who knew exactly what she was doing, right down to the counselor who testified that Carly had been reading Crime and Punishment, Dostoevsky’s novel about a planned killing, in the days before the shooting.

From the stand, her stepdad called her “just a sweet little girl.” He said he still believes she didn’t know who he was that day.

In August 2024, at 15, the jury convicted her on every count and the judge handed her life. Her lawyers took it all the way up. On August 20, 2026, the Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and the life sentences, finding no reversible errors in her trial. The verdict stands.

The case in short:
• Carly Gregg, 14 at the time, Rankin County, Mississippi
• Victim: her mother, Ashley Smylie, 40, a teacher at Carly’s own school
• Weapon: a .357 revolver kept under the mattress, on her mom’s side of the bed
• Three shots to her mother; stepdad Heath Smylie shot in the shoulder, survived, and wrestled the gun away
• Her defense: she was hearing voices, and new medication made her worse
• The state: she knew exactly what she was doing — down to the Crime and Punishment she’d been reading before it
• She turned down a 40-year plea and went to trial
• August 2024, age 15: guilty on every count, sentenced to life
• August 2026: the Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed — the verdict stands

She was 14. She walked her own mother into a bedroom and put three rounds in her. Then she picked up the phone and lured her stepdad home.

A jury called it m*rder. The Mississippi Supreme Court just agreed.

The only one still calling her a “sweet little girl” is the man she tried to k*ll.

So spare me the “sick kid.” What would you call her?

text:
A 14-year-old girl shot her mother three times at home. Then she picked up her mom’s phone and texted her stepdad: “Are you almost home, honey?” He walked in 49 minutes later. At trial she was offered a deal for 40 years. She turned it down, and the jury gave her this:

Life in prison. Her name is Carly Gregg, and in August the Mississippi Supreme Court upheld the sentence. Her mother was a teacher, and the whole thing started with something a school friend told her that afternoon:

Carly was hiding weed and secret phones in her bedroom. A few hours later her mother was dead.

On March 19, 2024, in Brandon, Mississippi, Carly took a .357 Magnum from under her parents’ mattress. The home cameras recorded her walking through the house with the gun hidden behind her back. Then three shots.

After that she texted a friend to come over. When her stepdad Heath opened the front door, she started firing. One bullet hit him less than six inches from his face. He wrestled the gun away from her, and she ran out the back door with the friend. Police later found one of the kitchen cameras hidden inside the refrigerator.

In court the prosecutor repeated what Carly said that day: “I put three in my mom and I got three more waiting for my stepdad.” Her lawyers argued that a new antidepressant had pushed her into a mental health crisis. The state’s psychiatrist said she understood exactly what she was doing. The jury found her guilty in about two hours.

In the video below, Carly stands at the podium while the judge reads the verdict: guilty on all three counts. She cries. Less than an hour later the same jury gives her life in prison, and when the judge reads it out she doesn’t cry at all. She just nods.

So people split on this one: is life in prison right for a girl who planned an ambush, faked a text and hid the camera, or should a 14-year-old on brand-new medication get a chance to walk out one day?

text:
This week, global business and political leaders are converging in #Shenzhen for a pivotal moment in regional diplomacy. On November 17–18, the #APEC CEO Summit 2026 will open at the Qianhai International Conference Center, setting the stage for the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 18–19. Marking China’s third turn as APEC host—following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014—and the most significant diplomatic event in the opening year of its 15th Five-Year Plan, the Shenzhen gathering arrives at a critical juncture. For a global economy weighed down by sluggish recovery and geopolitical fragmentation, the meeting offers a timely test of whether the Asia-Pacific can remain a pillar of stability and shared growth.

The central question facing the region is straightforward: where does Asia-Pacific cooperation go from here? Together, APEC's 21 member economies account for more than 60 percent of global GDP and nearly half of world trade, making the region the undisputed engine of global growth. Yet that engine faces growing headwinds—from rising unilateralism and protectionism to the increasing politicization of trade and industrial and supply chains. At such a moment, steering the region toward steady, open cooperation is essential. As the world's second-largest economy, China contributes over 60 percent of Asia-Pacific economic growth and serves as the largest trading partner for 13 APEC member economies. By setting "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together" as the theme for the 2026 APEC "China Year," with "Openness, Innovation, Cooperation" as its three priorities, Beijing is making a clear case against decoupling and zero-sum rivalry.

Perhaps the clearest signal of confidence comes from the private sector, which has voted with its feet. More than 2,000 political and business leaders are attending the APEC CEO Summit 2026, representing all 21 APEC member economies alongside major enterprises from 13 non-APEC economies, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Switzerland. Notably, 115 Fortune Global 500 companies are represented in Qianhai—with US firms accounting for nearly 20 percent of participating enterprises from economies other than China, the largest international contingent. That level of turnout underscores a practical reality: multinational businesses still view the Asia-Pacific as indispensable, and they remain eager to tap into the opportunities of China's continuous opening-up and industrial modernization.

Historically, this year's summit also marks an important inflection point. Over the past quarter-century—from the 2001 Shanghai Accord to the 2014 Beijing Agenda and the Beijing Roadmap for APEC's Contribution to the Realization of the FTAAP, which formally launched the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) process—China’s role within APEC has evolved from participant to agenda-setter. Appropriately, 2026 marks both the 20th anniversary of the FTAAP vision and the final review year of the APEC Connectivity Blueprint for 2015–2025. Rather than settling for broad declarations, the Shenzhen agenda is geared toward concrete deliverables: the CEO Summit will issue the APEC CEO Summit Shenzhen Initiative 2026—the first such outcome document in its 30-year history—while leaders are set to advance practical frameworks for digital trade, cross-border data verification, an open and inclusive AI innovation ecosystem, and the digital and green transition, laying actionable groundwork toward the APEC Putrajaya Vision 2040.

Choosing Shenzhen as the host city carries unmistakable symbolism. Once a quiet coastal town, Shenzhen transformed into a global hub of technology and trade through China’s reform and opening-up—its rise mirroring the broader "Asia-Pacific miracle." Today, anchored by the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area's blend of world-class physical infrastructure and regulatory connectivity, the city serves as a natural bridge between China and the Pacific Rim. The international delegates' firsthand exposure to Shenzhen's tech firms, green industrial parks, and urban dynamism allows the world to see China's innovation-driven growth up close—and turn dialogue into tangible, mutually beneficial partnerships.

Great eras demand broad vision and pragmatic leadership. As leaders gather in Shenzhen, the upcoming summit is both a reaffirmation of China's commitment to high-standard opening-up and a vital opportunity for APEC member economies to rebuild consensus. Guided by the forthcoming Shenzhen Declaration, the region has a chance to choose openness over barriers, innovation over stagnation, and cooperation over division—writing the next chapter of the Asia-Pacific growth story.

text:
THE EZE 25 | WEEK 11: WHY EACH TEAM IS HERE

Here is the case for every team in this week's Eze 25. Résumé and performance rankings refer to our model. The full season drives the ranking; recent games illustrate the case.

1. GEORGIA (9-1)
Georgia keeps the crown after following its 42–7 win at Ole Miss with a 48–21 victory over Missouri. Add the road win at Alabama, and the Bulldogs have both heavyweight victories and dominant margins. They lead our performance ratings and sit fourth in résumé. The next challenge is a trip to South Carolina.

2. NOTRE DAME (9-1)
The Irish backed up their 31–24 win over Miami by handling Boston College 41–7. Second in performance and fifth in résumé gives Notre Dame a strong case near the top, and its head-to-head win settles the close comparison with Miami. SMU visits South Bend next.

3. MIAMI (9-1)
Miami answered its first loss with a 36–25 win over Duke. Road victories at Wake Forest and Clemson help give the Hurricanes our third-best résumé, backed by the fourth-best performance rating. Notre Dame’s head-to-head victory decides their order. Miami hosts Virginia Tech next with plenty still within reach.

4. UTAH (10-0)
Utah keeps finding ways to win. The Utes followed a 28–20 victory over BYU by surviving Arizona 40–39 on the road, preserving a perfect record and our No. 1 résumé. Their eighth-place performance rating explains why the blend lands them fourth. Next comes another road test at TCU.

5. ALABAMA (8-2)
Alabama has stacked road wins at LSU, 31–13, and Vanderbilt, 21–6. Its No. 3 performance rating carries more weight in our blend than its No. 11 résumé. The losses to Georgia and Tennessee still count; Tennessee’s head-to-head win falls outside our fixed two-point model-score window. Chattanooga visits next.

6. TEXAS (8-2)
Texas escaped Baton Rouge with a 22–21 win, adding another road victory to a résumé that already includes Ohio State, Tennessee and Ole Miss. Sixth in résumé and seventh in performance puts the Longhorns firmly in this group, while losses to Oklahoma and Florida limit their climb. Arkansas comes to Austin next.

7. INDIANA (9-1)
Indiana strengthened its case with a 27–13 win over USC, its third straight victory since a four-point loss to Ohio State. The Hoosiers have our seventh-best résumé and tenth-best performance rating, a balanced foundation for No. 7. A trip to Washington is the next chance to add another road win.

8. WAKE FOREST (9-1)
Wake Forest made a statement by going to SMU and winning 49–7. That is seven straight victories since the Miami loss, with a road win at Louisville also strengthening the résumé. Eighth in résumé and eleventh in performance brings the Deacons to No. 8. Georgia Tech awaits in Atlanta.

9. OHIO STATE (7-3)
Ohio State stopped a two-game skid by beating Northwestern 28–19. Road wins at Indiana and Iowa support its No. 6 performance rating, while three losses leave its résumé at No. 16. Oregon won their matchup, but their 2.75-point model gap exceeds our two-point head-to-head window. Next: at Nebraska.

10. TENNESSEE (8-2)
Tennessee followed its 34–6 win over Kentucky with a 22–7 road victory at Texas A&M. The 26–10 win over Alabama remains a major achievement, while three-point losses to Texas and South Carolina hurt the résumé. Ninth in performance and thirteenth in résumé puts the Vols tenth. LSU visits Neyland next.

11. UCLA (10-0)
UCLA keeps winning, reaching 10–0 with a 22–14 victory over Illinois. The Bruins’ perfect record and road win at Oregon earn our second-best résumé. Their opponent-adjusted performance ranks twenty-first, which pulls the combined ranking to No. 11. Michigan in Ann Arbor offers another opportunity to strengthen that case.

12. TEXAS TECH (9-1)
Texas Tech’s offense keeps producing, following a 53–48 win over West Virginia with a 52–27 road victory at Oklahoma State. The Red Raiders own our tenth-best résumé, but defensive ups and downs and the Cincinnati loss help explain their fifteenth-place performance rating. They head to Baylor at No. 12.

13. OREGON (7-3)
Oregon is building momentum: a 41–28 win at Ohio State followed by a 31–7 victory over Michigan makes three straight wins. Victories over Boise State and USC add substance, although three losses still weigh on the full-season case. Thirteenth in performance and fifteenth in résumé puts Oregon here. Michigan State is next on the road Friday.

14. IOWA (8-2)
Iowa has outscored Wisconsin, Northwestern and Purdue 82–17 across three straight wins. That run supports a fourteenth-place performance rating, while losses to Ohio State and Minnesota leave its résumé eighteenth. The Hawkeyes have earned their place in this middle group and now travel to Illinois.

15. BYU (8-2)
BYU’s 28–24 win over Notre Dame remains one of the strongest results on this board. A 28–7 victory over Baylor got the Cougars moving again after the Utah loss, but defeats against Utah and UCF still matter. Twelfth in résumé and twentieth in performance lands BYU fifteenth. Kansas is next on the road.

16. BOISE STATE (9-1)
Boise State has won nine straight since its seven-point loss at Oregon, most recently edging Oregon State 46–41. That consistency earns our ninth-best résumé. Close escapes against Texas State and Oregon State help explain a twenty-third-place performance rating and the No. 16 overall placement. San Diego State visits next.

17. OLE MISS (6-4)
Ole Miss has taken two straight losses, most recently 24–17 at Oklahoma, but wins over LSU and Louisville still give it meaningful results. Its twelfth-place performance rating keeps it in the Top 25, and the 32–24 head-to-head win over LSU puts the Rebels immediately ahead of the Tigers. Wofford is next.

18. LSU (6-4)
LSU is one of this poll’s toughest placements. Big wins over Clemson, Texas A&M and Auburn support a fifth-place performance rating, but four losses leave its résumé thirty-seventh. The latest was 22–21 against Texas, and the head-to-head loss to Ole Miss keeps LSU behind the Rebels. A trip to Tennessee offers a chance to improve that résumé.

19. ARIZONA (7-3)
Arizona pushed unbeaten Utah to the limit in a 40–39 loss. Earlier wins of 34–7 over Cincinnati and 39–3 over Iowa State help explain its seventeenth-place performance rating. Three losses leave the résumé twenty-seventh, producing a No. 19 overall finish this week. Kansas State awaits in Manhattan.

20. LOUISVILLE (7-3)
Louisville has won five straight after edging North Carolina 16–14 on the road. All three losses came by exactly three points, keeping its performance profile competitive even as the losses hurt its résumé. Eighteenth in performance and twenty-ninth in résumé brings the Cardinals to No. 20. Pittsburgh visits next.

21. USC (7-3)
USC’s 30–18 win over Ohio State gives the Trojans a result worth respecting. The latest 27–13 loss at Indiana adds to earlier double-digit defeats against Oregon and Wisconsin, limiting their consistency. Twenty-second in résumé and twenty-seventh in performance produces No. 21 in the combined field. Maryland visits the Coliseum next.

22. DUKE (7-3)
Duke’s 47–2 win over Boston College and 41–3 victory at NC State showed how convincing it can be. A 36–25 loss at Miami interrupted that run, while earlier defeats against Georgia Tech and North Carolina weigh on the résumé. Its twenty-second-place performance rating helps keep Duke ranked. Clemson visits Friday.

23. HOUSTON (7-3)
Houston’s wins over Oklahoma State and Cincinnati keep it in the conversation, and it stayed within one score of both Texas Tech and Utah. A 42–32 loss at Colorado weakened the case this week. Twenty-sixth in résumé and twenty-eighth in performance combines into No. 23 across this field. Next: at West Virginia.

24. NORTHWESTERN (6-4)
Northwestern stays ranked despite three straight losses, most recently 28–19 at Ohio State. Wins of 41–7 over Colorado and 34–13 over Penn State still support a sixteenth-place performance rating. Its forty-ninth-place résumé explains why it is close to the cutoff. A trip to Minnesota brings a chance to stop the slide.

25. NEW MEXICO (8-2)
New Mexico holds the final spot after a 21–17 loss to UNLV. Eight wins, including victories over North Dakota State and Nevada, keep its résumé twenty-fifth. A thirty-second-place performance rating leaves the Lobos with little separation from the teams chasing them. Friday’s trip to Wyoming is the next test.

text:
Every first grader in Japan carries the same backpack for six years.

It's called a randoseru. Stiff leather. A box with straps. It costs about four hundred dollars, it comes with a six-year warranty, and by tradition, the grandparents buy it.

Japanese grandparents start shopping more than a year in advance. It even has a name. "Ran-katsu." Randoseru hunting. Department stores hold events. Grandparents line up before opening. It is the most competitive thing old people do in this country.

My neighbor, Mr. Kimura, is 71. He spent forty years as a railway engineer. Japanese trains are on time partly because of men like Mr. Kimura. He irons his handkerchiefs.

His daughter's husband grew up in Montana. They have a son, Eito. Three years ago, Eito turned five.

Mr. Kimura began ran-katsu fourteen months early. He visited nine stores. He made a spreadsheet. He reserved the perfect one, in navy, and told the family.

Then the phone rang. Montana.

Eito's other grandfather. Warren. Seventy-four at the time. A saddlemaker for fifty-one years. He has made saddles for ranchers, rodeo champions, and one governor. He had never made anything for a five-year-old.

"No grandson of mine," Warren said, "is carrying a backpack I didn't make."

What followed was the most polite war ever fought across the Pacific.

Mr. Kimura emailed Warren a list of official requirements. Through his daughter. Weight. Dimensions. Must fit standard A4 paper. Reflective strip. Child-safe clasp. Six-year durability.

Warren had to look up what A4 was. He thought it was a highway.

Then he wrote back one line.

"Six years? My saddles last sixty."

Mr. Kimura did not cancel his reservation. Instead, he mailed Warren a sample randoseru. For reference.

Warren took it apart with a seam ripper to see how it was built, and emailed Mr. Kimura a picture: every piece laid out on his workbench like evidence.

Mr. Kimura did not sleep that night.

Warren went out to his shop.

He worked on it all winter. Every night after supper. His hands are not what they were. His wife says some nights he could only work an hour before he had to put them in warm water.

He tooled the leather by hand, the way he does a show saddle. Oak leaves. Wild roses. Under the flap, Eito's name in Japanese letters, which took him eleven tries on scrap leather before he got them right. The rivets are brass. The stitching is the same thread he uses on saddles that hold a grown man on a bucking horse.

In February, it arrived in Japan.

Mr. Kimura inspected it like a customs officer.

He measured it. It fit A4 paper exactly. He weighed it. Two hundred grams over. He wrote this down. Under it, after some thought, he wrote: "Acceptable." He opened and closed the clasp one hundred times, counting out loud. The clasp did not care.

Then he set it on the living room table and stared at it. Twenty minutes. Silent.

The next morning, he called the department store and quietly cancelled the navy one.

He called Warren that night. Mr. Kimura doesn't speak English. Warren doesn't speak Japanese. His daughter translated.

Mr. Kimura said one word. "Shokunin."

In Japan, that is the highest thing you can call a man who works with his hands. It means a craftsman who has given his whole life to doing one thing right. We don't say it lightly. In forty years on the railway, Mr. Kimura had not once used it on anybody.

His daughter explained what it meant.

Montana went quiet. Nothing on the line but breathing.

Then Warren said, "Tell him thank you. Tell him his trains are pretty good too."

And then, after a while, the only explanation he ever offered:

"A kid ought to carry something every day that was made by somebody who loves him. So he never has to wonder."

In April, Eito walked into a school where six hundred kids carried identical randoseru.

And one saddle.

Kids crowded around him. They touched the oak leaves. One of them smelled it. Then they all smelled it. The teacher had to break it up. By May, nobody at that school called Eito "the half-American kid" anymore.

He was "Cowboy." He considers this a promotion.

Eito is in third grade now. Most randoseru are scratched and dented by this point. His looks better every year. Leather does that, Warren says, when somebody uses it every day. "Like a good marriage."

Warren doesn't make saddles anymore. His hands are done. Nothing has come out of his shop since that randoseru.

But every Sunday night, on video, he teaches Eito how to oil the leather. Small circles. Slow. "Like you're petting a horse."

Eito has never petted a horse. He has become extremely good at it anyway.

Last month, Mr. Kimura knocked on my door with a pen and a sheet of paper. He needed a letter written to Montana. In English. He had a question he couldn't ask through his daughter.

He wanted to know if there was a warranty.

Warren's answer came back in a week. A photo of the inside of the flap, behind the lining, where no one would ever look.

Stamped into the leather, very small:

"W. HOLT, SADDLEMAKER. GUARANTEED 60 YEARS."

And under it, smaller:

"OR UNTIL HE NEEDS ONE FOR HIS OWN KID. WHICHEVER COMES FIRST."

Mr. Kimura read it two times over. He set his glasses down on the counter. Alone in his kitchen, out loud, he said it again.

"Shokunin."

That makes twice. Ever.

He has printed the photo. It's on his refrigerator, next to the train schedule.

In Japan, a randoseru is built to last until a child grows up.

In Montana, a grandfather built one to last until that child grows old.
